job_statement: When I have installed the OpenShift CLI, I want to configure it for my shell environment and cluster access, so I can work efficiently with tab completion, authentication, and persistent settings.
related_jobs: Get started with the OpenShift CLI
desired_outcomes: Minimize the time spent typing full CLI commands by enabling shell auto-completion
Reduce errors when entering oc commands by having the shell suggest valid options
Ensure cluster credentials are accessible across terminal sessions without re-authenticating
evidence: cli_reference-combined.adoc, lines 2126-2680 (Configuring the OpenShift CLI assembly including tab completion and kubeconfig access)
notes: This main_job covers the initial post-install configuration steps. It bridges the gap between installation (chunk 1) and daily usage. The section is relatively short, suggesting configuration is lightweight compared to installation.

job_statement: When I am using the OpenShift CLI in a Bash or Zsh shell, I want to enable tab completion, so I can auto-complete commands and flags without memorizing every option.
desired_outcomes: Minimize the number of keystrokes needed to enter oc commands
Reduce the frequency of command syntax errors caused by mistyped flags or resource names
Minimize the time spent looking up available subcommands and options
evidence: cli_reference-combined.adoc, lines 2540-2619 (Enabling tab completion for Bash at line 2553 and Zsh at line 2591)
notes: Two parallel procedures exist for Bash and Zsh. The Bash procedure requires the bash-completion package as an additional prerequisite. The Zsh procedure is self-contained. Both procedures are short and mechanical.

section: Accessing kubeconfig by using the oc CLI
job_statement: When I need to access my OpenShift cluster from the command line or share cluster credentials, I want to export and configure a kubeconfig file, so I can authenticate to the cluster across sessions and machines.
prerequisites: Have access to the OpenShift API server endpoint
desired_outcomes: Minimize the number of times I need to re-authenticate when opening new terminal sessions
Reduce the risk of credential exposure by storing kubeconfig securely
Ensure the exported kubeconfig provides working cluster access from any machine
evidence: cli_reference-combined.adoc, lines 2629-2680 (Accessing kubeconfig by using the oc CLI procedure)
notes: The section includes an important security warning about storing kubeconfig securely and avoiding source control. This bridges configuration and profile management, since the kubeconfig file is the foundation for CLI profiles.

section: Usage of oc and kubectl commands
job_statement: When I am deciding which CLI tool to use for interacting with my OpenShift cluster, I want to understand the differences between oc and kubectl, so I can choose the right tool and leverage OpenShift-specific features when needed.
related_jobs: Get started with the OpenShift CLI
desired_outcomes: Minimize the likelihood of using a tool that lacks needed capabilities for OpenShift-specific resources
Reduce confusion about when to use oc versus kubectl for a given task
Minimize compatibility issues between oc client versions and cluster server versions
evidence: cli_reference-combined.adoc, lines 2683-3186 (Usage of oc and kubectl commands assembly, including The oc binary concept at line 3104 and The kubectl binary concept at line 3171)
notes: This is primarily conceptual content explaining that oc extends kubectl with OpenShift-specific features (DeploymentConfig, BuildConfig, Route, ImageStream, built-in login, new-app, new-project). Includes a version compatibility matrix. The kubectl binary section notes it is included when installing the OpenShift CLI. Most of the line range is attribute definitions repeated for the assembly.

job_statement: When I work with multiple OpenShift clusters or user accounts, I want to manage CLI profiles and contexts, so I can switch between environments without losing configuration or re-entering credentials.
related_jobs: Get started with the OpenShift CLI
desired_outcomes: Minimize the time spent re-authenticating when switching between clusters or projects
Reduce the risk of running commands against the wrong cluster or namespace
Ensure all cluster and user configurations are persisted and easily retrievable
evidence: cli_reference-combined.adoc, lines 3187-3930 (Managing CLI profiles assembly including context switching, manual configuration, and load/merge rules)
notes: This main_job covers the full lifecycle of CLI profile management. It assumes the user has already logged in at least once. The kubeconfig file (~/.kube/config) is automatically created on first login and serves as the foundation for all profile management.

job_statement: When I need to work in a different project or cluster, I want to switch CLI contexts, so I can target the correct environment without modifying configuration files manually.
prerequisites: Log in to at least one OpenShift cluster
desired_outcomes: Minimize the number of steps required to switch from one project or cluster to another
Reduce the risk of accidentally running commands in the wrong project or cluster
Minimize the time spent verifying which context is currently active
evidence: cli_reference-combined.adoc, lines 3607-3719 (About switching between CLI profiles concept, including kubeconfig structure example and oc project/oc status verification commands)
notes: This section explains the kubeconfig file structure (clusters, contexts, current-context, users) with a concrete YAML example. It covers using oc login, oc project, oc status, and oc config view for context management. Includes a note about logging back in as system:admin.

job_statement: When I need fine-grained control over my CLI configuration, I want to manually set clusters, contexts, and user entries using oc config commands, so I can create custom profiles that match my workflow without relying solely on interactive login.
prerequisites: Log in to at least one OpenShift cluster
desired_outcomes: Minimize the effort required to set up CLI profiles for multiple clusters and users
Reduce the risk of configuration errors by using structured oc config subcommands instead of editing files directly
Ensure all oc config subcommands (set-cluster, set-context, use-context, set, unset, view) are understood and available
evidence: cli_reference-combined.adoc, lines 3728-3874 (Manually configuring CLI profiles procedure at line 3728 and Manual configuration reference table at line 3806)
notes: The procedure section notes this is advanced usage and that most users can rely on oc login and oc project. The reference table documents six oc config subcommands: set-cluster, set-context, use-context, set, unset, and view. This is where users with complex multi-cluster setups will spend the most time.

job_statement: When I have multiple kubeconfig files or override options, I want to understand how the CLI loads and merges configuration, so I can predict which context, cluster, and user credentials will be used for a given command.
desired_outcomes: Minimize unexpected behavior caused by conflicting configuration sources
Reduce debugging time when the CLI uses the wrong cluster or credentials
Ensure understanding of the precedence order: --config flag, then $KUBECONFIG env var, then ~/.kube/config
evidence: cli_reference-combined.adoc, lines 3882-3921 (Load and merge rules concept explaining configuration file hierarchy, context determination, cluster and user resolution)
notes: This is purely conceptual content with no procedures. It documents the merge precedence: --config flag wins, then $KUBECONFIG (which can be a colon-separated list of paths), then ~/.kube/config as default. Context is resolved via --context flag, then current-context in config, then empty. Users can only have one auth technique per user entry. Gap: no troubleshooting guidance for when merge rules produce unexpected results.
